stories.headline: Jeffries shredded over Hegseth impeachment snafu as Dem jockeys for speaker's gavel
stories.note: Jeffries takes heat over the failed Hegseth impeachment push just as he angles for the speaker's gavel.
body: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is taking criticism from his own side after two embarrassing floor moments this week, just as he campaigns to become Speaker when Democrats take the majority in January.

The first came Tuesday evening, when 11 House Democrats were absent for a procedural vote on Rep. Thomas Massie's resolution to impeach War Secretary Pete Hegseth. Had only seven of them shown up, the GOP motion to kill the resolution would have failed and forced a debate and likely an impeachment vote.

Rep. Melanie Stansbury said she and others were stuck in traffic, though several reports placed the missing members at a fundraiser under two miles from the Capitol. The next day, a bill Democratic leaders were urging members to oppose passed by unanimous voice vote because no Democrat asked for a recorded vote.

Progressive voices piled on. Demand Progress director Sean Vitka said Democratic leaders "failed to deliver and handed Republicans a win," and Fred Trump III, the president's Democratic nephew, said he may rethink his support for Jeffries.

Other Democrats defended Jeffries. Strategist Mike Nellis said nobody is running against him, incoming Majority Leader Katherine Clark said members need to show up on time, and Rep. Jared Moskowitz said the misses weren't leadership's fault.
Why it matters: Democrats are about to run the House, and their first big moves already look disorganized, giving Republicans an early storyline about whether Jeffries' team is ready to lead.

stories.headline: Sen Bernie Sanders supports Chris Van Hollen's bid to challenge Schumer for Senate Democratic leader post
stories.note: Democrats are fighting each other over Schumer's job instead of uniting after their wins.
body: Sen. Bernie Sanders is backing Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland in his newly launched challenge to Chuck Schumer for the job of Senate Democratic leader.

Van Hollen announced his run Thursday, saying Democrats need new leadership to deliver on what voters asked for. Sanders, who had already said he would not support Schumer for another term, endorsed him the same day, as did Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed.
Schumer is fighting to keep the post and become majority leader next year. He touted "55 seats and counting" and insisted he already has the votes to stay on as leader.

The Republican National Committee jumped on the fight. Press secretary Natalie Baldassarre called it a "leadership brawl" that previews a Democratic agenda of "chaos, infighting" and a race to the far left.

Why it matters: Rather than unifying after their election gains, Senate Democrats are heading into a public leadership fight between their establishment and progressive wings, which Republicans can use to paint the new majority as divided.

stories.headline: Mamdani prepares to fulfill promise to axe NYPD unit responsible for controlling protest violence
stories.note: Mamdani's move to cut an NYPD protest unit hands Republicans a ready-made public safety contrast.
body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist, is reportedly getting ready to announce that he will disband the NYPD's Strategic Response Group, a unit that handles protests, civil disturbances, major events and counterterrorism work.

According to Politico, City Hall has weighed moving the unit under Mamdani's new Office of Community Safety, and the change could come through an executive order. A mayoral spokesperson confirmed the administration will disband the group and separate protest response from counterterrorism.

The NYPD calls the unit a critical asset for parades, protests and big events, and says it also responds to shootings, bank robberies and areas with rising crime. Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch told the City Council in March that the unit isn't used for peaceful protests, only those involving criminal activity, and was present at roughly 6% of the city's 4,255 protests in 2025.

Mamdani has argued that counterterrorism and protest response shouldn't be handled by the same unit, calling the change his long-stated "vision." It's still unclear what would replace the unit's duties.
Why it matters: Cutting a police unit built to handle unruly crowds hands Republicans a fresh, concrete example of the public safety risks that come with far-left Democratic leadership in big cities.

stories.headline: Texas Democrats put DEI back on agenda after sweeping to power
stories.note: Newly empowered Texas Democrats are reviving DEI fights, a contrast Republicans can run on.
body: After big gains in Texas, Democrats are opening their new state House majority with bills, HB 358 and SB 125, to repeal the state's 2023 law banning DEI offices and programs at public universities.

The repeal faces long odds because Republicans kept control of the Texas Senate. The 2023 law, signed by Gov. Greg Abbott, led the UT System alone to close 21 DEI offices, eliminate 311 positions and cancel 681 contracts, programs and trainings.

Conservative policy experts warn Democrats could still weaken the ban without repealing it. Many university regents' terms expire Feb. 1, 2027, giving Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa a chance to appoint new board members, though the GOP Senate must confirm them and current regents can hold over until 2029 if it doesn't.

Chuck DeVore of the Texas Public Policy Foundation said the repeal is unlikely to reach the governor's desk and that his group would sue to make sure the law is followed. The Democratic bill sponsors didn't respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Why it matters: Texas Democrats campaigned on Iran, immigration and affordability, but their first move is reviving a culture-war fight over DEI, and the Republican state Senate remains a firewall against it.

stories.headline: Trump asks Vance to focus on 'corruption and crime' in Dem-run cities, states
stories.note: Trump puts Vance on offense against crime and corruption in Democrat-run places.
body: President Trump said Thursday he has asked Vice President JD Vance to give his "complete and total attention" to corruption and crime in Democrat-run cities and states.

In a Truth Social post, Trump named Minnesota, California and Illinois as examples and claimed billions of dollars are being stolen every month, saying the budget could be balanced by fixing it. He did not give specific examples to back up those figures.

Vance already leads the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, created by a March executive order targeting fraud in federal benefit programs. In October the task force was preparing charges against more than 40 defendants in an alleged $40 million SNAP fraud scheme.

The task force says it has identified $260.7 billion in suspected fraud and prevented about $72 billion a year in potentially fraudulent payments, though Fox notes those numbers haven't been independently verified. It isn't yet clear if the new directive expands Vance's role.
Why it matters: With Democrats about to control Congress, Trump is keeping the focus on fraud and crime in blue states, an issue where Republicans believe they have the stronger hand.

stories.headline: The top Trump officials Democrats admit are on their hit list for investigations in the new Congress
stories.note: Democrats are openly planning an investigation spree, feeding the GOP's overreach message.
body: Democrats are openly naming the Trump administration officials they want to investigate, and possibly impeach, once they take control of Congress in January.

Beyond War Secretary Pete Hegseth, lawmakers told Fox News Digital they are eyeing Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and border czar Tom Homan.

Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego said Democrats will hold everyone accountable, while admitting the details "remain to be seen." Rep. Ted Lieu, who is running for caucus chair, said he wants hearings and possible impeachment proceedings for Miller and Homan, and an investigation of Lutnick tied to allegations involving Nvidia's CEO and a suspected Chinese operative. Rep. Ro Khanna also wants to know what Rubio knew.

Fox notes no wrongdoing has been established in the allegations, and that removing an official requires a two-thirds vote in the Senate. Rep. Brian Mast said Democrats seem set on impeaching "anyone who was appointed by the president."

Why it matters: Before even taking the gavel, Democrats are signaling an investigation and impeachment spree, which plays straight into the Republican argument that they will put political vendettas ahead of governing.

stories.headline: Soldier who scolded Hegseth's entourage at Tomb of Unknown Soldier receives special honor from Pentagon chief
stories.note: Hegseth turns a viral moment into a classy salute to a soldier doing his duty.
body: War Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday awarded the Joint Service Commendation Medal to Spc. Thomas Iglesias, the Old Guard soldier who told his entourage to keep quiet at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Veterans Day.
Video showed Iglesias reminding the group to keep "an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times" after laughter was heard as Hegseth's party walked away following the ceremony.

Rather than bristling, Hegseth welcomed the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment to the Pentagon and pinned the medal on Iglesias for carrying out his duties. "We love soldiers. We love standards," Hegseth posted on X.

Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell had earlier said the soldier "correctly and respectfully" reminded everyone to maintain decorum, and that the department always honors the sacrifices of service members.
Why it matters: Hegseth turned an awkward viral moment into a public salute to military standards, a good look for him as Democrats push to impeach him.
